blocks.text: 1. Bayesian Networks

blocks.alt: Variable A leads to variable B, which leads to variable C

blocks.text: Naive Bayes, already covered in depth in the Classification module, made one deliberate, bold simplification: every feature is treated as conditionally independent of every other feature, given the class label, an assumption that made the underlying math tractable but rarely holds exactly true in real data. Bayesian Networks remove this assumption entirely, explicitly representing exactly which variables genuinely depend on which others, and precisely how strongly, rather than assuming blanket independence across the board.

This makes Bayesian Networks a genuinely more expressive, more general probabilistic modeling framework, still built directly on the same Bayes theorem foundation already covered for Naive Bayes, but capable of representing far richer, more realistic patterns of dependency between variables than Naive Bayes's deliberately simplified structure ever could.
2. The Graph Structure

blocks.alt: Nodes represent variables while edges represent dependencies

blocks.text: A Bayesian Network is represented as a directed graph, where every node corresponds to one variable in the model, and every edge represents a direct dependence relationship between two variables. An edge running from variable A to variable B means A directly influences B's probability distribution.

The absence of an edge between two variables carries genuine meaning too: it indicates those two variables are conditionally independent of each other, given whatever other connections they each have elsewhere in the network. This graph structure is not merely a visual aid; it directly, precisely encodes exactly which independence assumptions the model is actually making, in sharp contrast to Naive Bayes, which makes the same blanket independence assumption across every single feature pair without exception.
3. Directly Relaxing Naive Bayes's Assumption

blocks.alt: Naive Bayes assumes everything independent while a Bayesian network models real dependencies

blocks.text: It is worth connecting this directly back to Naive Bayes's core simplification, covered in depth in its own topic: every feature is treated as independent of every other feature, given the class. Bayesian Networks let some features genuinely, explicitly depend on each other, and represent that dependency directly as an edge in the graph, rather than assuming it away.

A classic illustrative example makes this concrete: whether the grass is wet genuinely depends on both whether it rained and whether a sprinkler was used, and these two causes are not independent of each other either, rain makes sprinkler use less likely in the first place. A Bayesian Network can represent this entire web of genuine dependencies directly and explicitly, a strictly more expressive model than Naive Bayes's simplified structure, though this expressiveness comes at the real cost of actually needing to specify, or learn, that dependency structure correctly in the first place.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: The classic wet-grass, rain, and sprinkler example is one of the most commonly used illustrative Bayesian Networks in textbooks and courses, specifically because it makes the genuine dependency between causes, rain reducing sprinkler use, immediately intuitive.

blocks.text: 4. Conditional Probability Tables

blocks.alt: A parent node value feeds a conditional probability table, producing the child node probability

blocks.text: Every single node in a Bayesian Network stores what is called a conditional probability table, specifying the probability of that node's own value, given every possible combination of values its direct parent nodes, the nodes with edges pointing directly into it, might take. A node with no parents at all simply stores its own overall, unconditional probability distribution, exactly the prior probability concept already covered in depth for Naive Bayes.

Multiplying these individual conditional probability tables together, following the graph's structure precisely, reconstructs the full joint probability distribution across every single variable in the entire network simultaneously. This is a genuinely elegant, compact way to represent a potentially enormous joint distribution, using only the local, node-by-node conditional relationships the graph structure actually specifies, rather than needing to store every possible combination of every variable directly.

blocks.text: 5. Inference: Reasoning Under Partial Observation

blocks.alt: Known variables feed inference, estimating the unknown variable

blocks.text: Once a Bayesian Network's structure and conditional probability tables are established, the network can be used for inference: given that some variables have actually been observed directly, compute the updated probability of other, unobserved variables. Observing that the grass is wet, for instance, allows the network to compute an updated probability of whether it actually rained.

This inference process is, at its mathematical core, exactly Bayes theorem, already covered in depth in the Naive Bayes topic, just applied repeatedly across an entire connected network of variables rather than a single class variable and a set of assumed-independent features. Observing evidence at one or more nodes propagates through the graph's dependency structure, updating the probability estimates at every connected node, exactly the kind of belief-updating-given-evidence reasoning Bayes theorem was originally built to perform.
6. A Causal Interpretation, With a Caveat

A Bayesian Network's edges are very often interpreted as representing genuine causal relationships, not merely statistical correlation, a distinction that has been implicit throughout much of this course whenever discussing what a model's learned patterns actually mean. In the classic wet-grass example, the edge from rain to wet grass is naturally read as rain causes wet grass, not merely rain happens to correlate with wet grass.

This causal reading is a genuinely useful, intuitive interpretive lens for building and understanding a Bayesian Network's structure, though it is worth stating directly that the underlying mathematics itself only strictly requires conditional dependence between connected variables, not true, verified causation. A Bayesian Network built purely from observed statistical patterns, without careful causal reasoning about which direction the true causal arrows actually point, can still function correctly for inference purposes, but its edges may not always represent genuine cause-and-effect relationships in the way they are commonly, informally interpreted.
7. Why the Name: Bayesian

It is worth being direct about where this technique's name actually comes from, connecting straight back to Bayes theorem, already covered in full depth in the Naive Bayes topic. Bayesian Networks are named specifically for their fundamental reliance on that exact same theorem for every single piece of inference they perform.

Every inference calculation carried out across a Bayesian Network, updating beliefs about unobserved variables given whatever evidence has actually been observed, is, at its mathematical core, a repeated, systematic application of Bayes theorem, propagated carefully across the graph's dependency structure. This naming convention directly parallels Naive Bayes's own name, both techniques are built on the identical theorem, differing specifically in how much independence they assume, blanket independence for Naive Bayes, versus an explicitly specified, generally far richer dependency structure for Bayesian Networks.
8. Building the Network Structure

blocks.alt: Domain knowledge or learning from data produces the network structure

blocks.text: A Bayesian Network's graph structure gets determined in one of two common ways. Expert-defined networks have their structure manually specified by a domain expert, drawing directly on real, established knowledge about which variables genuinely influence which others in a specific field, medical diagnosis being a classic example where a physician's understanding of disease and symptom relationships directly shapes the network's edges.

Learned networks instead use algorithms that search over possible graph structures, looking for whichever structure best explains the patterns actually observed in available data, useful whenever the true underlying dependency structure is not already well understood or well documented. Expert-defined structures tend to dominate in well-understood, high-stakes domains where getting the causal story right matters enormously, while learned structures tend to be used when exploring a genuinely new or poorly understood domain where no strong prior expert knowledge is readily available.

blocks.text: 9. When Bayesian Networks Are the Right Modeling Choice

Bayesian Networks are the right choice specifically when genuine, meaningful dependencies exist between features that Naive Bayes's blanket independence assumption, already covered in depth in its own topic, would distort badly if applied instead. They are also the right choice whenever explaining exactly why a particular prediction or conclusion was reached genuinely matters, since the graph structure itself is directly, transparently interpretable as an actual chain of reasoning, considerably more so than many of the other classifiers covered throughout this course.

They fit especially well in situations requiring reasoning under genuine uncertainty, where some variables are directly observed while others remain unobserved and must be inferred, medical diagnosis, risk assessment, and fault diagnosis systems all being classic, well-established real-world application domains for exactly this kind of probabilistic, partially-observed reasoning.
10. Worked Example
The example below builds the classic wet-grass Bayesian Network directly, defining its conditional probability tables and performing inference given observed evidence.

code.content:
from pgmpy.models import DiscreteBayesianNetwork
from pgmpy.factors.discrete import TabularCPD
from pgmpy.inference import VariableElimination

# Structure: Rain and Sprinkler both influence WetGrass
model = DiscreteBayesianNetwork([('Rain', 'WetGrass'), ('Sprinkler', 'WetGrass'), ('Rain', 'Sprinkler')])

cpd_rain = TabularCPD(variable='Rain', variable_card=2, values=[[0.8], [0.2]])  # P(no rain)=0.8, P(rain)=0.2

# Sprinkler depends on Rain: less likely to be used if it already rained
cpd_sprinkler = TabularCPD(
    variable='Sprinkler', variable_card=2,
    values=[[0.6, 0.99], [0.4, 0.01]],  # columns: Rain=No, Rain=Yes
    evidence=['Rain'], evidence_card=[2]
)

# WetGrass depends on both Rain and Sprinkler
cpd_wetgrass = TabularCPD(
    variable='WetGrass', variable_card=2,
    values=[[1.0, 0.1, 0.1, 0.01], [0.0, 0.9, 0.9, 0.99]],
    evidence=['Rain', 'Sprinkler'], evidence_card=[2, 2]
)

model.add_cpds(cpd_rain, cpd_sprinkler, cpd_wetgrass)

inference = VariableElimination(model)
result = inference.query(variables=['Rain'], evidence={'WetGrass': 1})
print("P(Rain | WetGrass=observed wet):")
print(result)

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Observing WetGrass=1, wet, updates the inferred probability of Rain noticeably higher than its 0.2 prior, exactly the belief-updating-given-evidence process covered throughout this topic, computed here through repeated application of Bayes theorem across the network's structure.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Bayesian Networks explicitly represent which variables depend on which others, removing Naive Bayes's blanket independence assumption.
The graph structure directly encodes dependence, an edge, and conditional independence, its absence.
Every node stores a conditional probability table over its own value given its parent nodes' values.
Multiplying these local tables together, following the graph structure, reconstructs the full joint probability distribution.
Inference computes updated probabilities of unobserved variables given observed evidence, a repeated application of Bayes theorem.
Edges are often interpreted causally, a useful lens, though the underlying math only strictly requires conditional dependence.
The network's structure can be manually specified by a domain expert, or learned algorithmically from observed data.
They fit genuine feature dependencies, explainability needs, and reasoning under partial observation, as in medical diagnosis.
